newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FOCUS-S.Korea C/A figures may not mean recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Korea C/A figures may not mean recovery.

text.p: South Korea's current account deficit narrowed in April from a year earlier, but economists warned on Thursday that slowing imports of capital goods could delay a hoped for recovery.

The nation's current account deficit narrowed to $1.71 billion in April from $2.36 billion a year earlier, largely because of increased shipments of heavy industrial goods, preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK) show.
But economists cautioned against excessive optimism. They said slowing imports of capital goods contributed to reducing the deficit, but could bode ill for economic recovery.
"Despite an improvement in April, it is still hard to see an economic recovery," said Lee Choon-yul, an economist at the Korea Institute of Finance.
"Slowing imports were the result of sagging capital investment and weak consumption. Conditions are unlikely to worsen, but it is too early to be optimistic about the overall economy."
The central bank figures showed the trade deficit on a balance of payments basis fell to $798.9 million in April from $1.58 billion a year ago.

"Exports of heavy industrial goods, especially electronic products, chemicals and vehicles, picked up in April on the strength of recovering global demand," said Paeng Dong-joon, director of the bank's statistics division.
He said import growth slowed in line with slowing demand in the domestic market.
"The trend of a shrinking deficit looks firm. So we will be seeing the deficit controlled within our earlier target of $18 billion this year," Paeng said.

Kim Joon-kyong, economist with the state-funded Korea Development Institute, said he would "cautiously" predict the deficit would continue to narrow. "That trend will be more conspicuous next year because of the high yen," Kim said.
Private-sector analysts said they saw no trend yet.

"I'm happy to see a shrinking deficit. But it is going to take time to see a firm and reliable trend. Supply and demand conditions for semiconductors and petrochemicals still look unstable," said Cho Sung-keun, economist at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.

Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Research Institute, said: "It's better to wait a little longer before judging the export trend because international prices for South Korea's main products could fall again."
The BOK figures showed overall heavy industrial exports rose 7.2 percent in April, against a rise of 1.5 percent a year ago.

The central bank said exports of chemicals, including petrochemicals, on a customs-cleared basis, rose 19.4 percent in April from a year ago, compared with a fall of 10.2 percent recorded in April last year.

Overall imports on a customs-cleared basis rose 1.5 percent in the month, against a 14.3 percent rise a year earlier, the central bank said. Imports of capital goods increased 3.0 percent, raw materials 0.2 percent and consumer goods, including food, 2.8 percent.
The central bank said the growth of crude imports slowed to 15.9 percent in April from 35.5 percent a year ago.
The deficit in the invisible trade account rose to $877.5 million in April from $681.6 million a year ago, it said.
In the invisible trade account, payments rose to $3.47 billion in April from $3.16 billion a year ago, while revenues increased to $2.59 billion from $2.48 billion.
